item.title: The Three Core Artifacts in Agile
item.description:
In the previous installments of this series, we introduced the three main roles in Scrum. When it comes to actually implementing Scrum, there are also specific work objects or deliverables involved, and in Scrum these materials are called artifacts (Artifacts).

Artifacts

In Scrum, “artifacts” generally refers primarily to three core artifacts: the Product Backlog (PBI), the Sprint Backlog (SBI), and the Increment. But beyond these three core artifacts, there are in fact several other artifacts defined in relation to them.

In agile, artifacts serve as our work objects and deliverables. They should be jointly created and maintained by the entire Scrum Team, and they should be transparent to everyone—that is, these artifacts should be visible to everyone on the team. This is also an agile principle: it reinforces a shared understanding and communication across the team, so that everyone works on the same wavelength. Being transparent, visible, and available for reference at any time is extremely important.

Product Backlog (PBI)

The first core artifact is Product Backlog Items (PBI). A PBI is an ordered list containing all the unfinished items remaining for the product, including product requirements, unfixed bugs, technical optimizations, internal improvements, work tasks, and all kinds of product-related matters that the team needs to handle later.

PBIs should have the following important characteristics, otherwise known as the DEEP principles:

  • Detailed: detailed descriptions. Backlog items must have clear, unambiguous explanations so that team members can fully understand the necessary information about them. This is also why refinement is necessary in Scrum: the higher the priority, the more thorough the detailed description should be.
  • Emergent: emergent. The PBI is a dynamic list that can be inserted into and adjusted at any time as needed.
  • Estimated: estimated. Before a backlog item needs to be implemented, both the effort and the value to the product should be estimated. Whether these estimates are accurate is the foundation of the team’s actual productivity.
  • Prioritized: prioritized. The backlog items in a PBI should be ordered by priority; within a PBI, no two items have exactly the same priority. This is also an advantage of a list, since a list inherently has an ordering: in a PBI list, items higher up have higher priority. When the team pulls iteration tasks from the PBI, it also extracts them in order of priority.

Like other artifacts, although the PBI is also a deliverable that the team maintains together, the owner of the PBI is the PO (Product Owner). Other members do take part in adding details to the PBI, refining solutions, and the effort estimation for the PBI is also provided by the team, but ultimately only the PO is accountable for the PBI. The PO has the final say on interpretation and on prioritization.

During the creation and maintenance of the PBI, the PO usually brings as many relevant Features, Stories, and Enhancements (optimizations) as possible into the PBI as the basis for subsequent work. Then, after thorough communication with the team, typically through a product refinement meeting (grooming), the requirements are elaborated and implementation approaches are discussed. The team also breaks down concrete technical tasks and estimates the effort required.

The PBI is therefore essentially the source of Scrum agile development, playing a role comparable to the PRD, the main deliverable of the requirements breakdown phase in traditional development. The PBI is the foundation for launching a Sprint and also the source of the SBI.

Product Vision

Paired with the PBI, there is actually another supporting artifact, called in the Scrum definition the PBI’s commitment (the committed deliverable). That is the Product Vision.

The Product Vision is something that should be defined early in a product’s life. It mainly summarizes, at a high level, what goals the product aims to achieve, what purpose the thing everyone is building together is meant to serve, and what value it brings to users. In other words, it lets the whole team know what they are working for.

It is a relatively long-term description of the entire product roadmap.

Sprint Backlog (SBI)

Sprint means a short burst. It is a short, time-boxed window defined in Scrum, within which the team can complete some deliverable product features. Based on the completed features, it gathers feedback from relevant stakeholders so that the product’s evolution roadmap can be adjusted in a timely manner. It is a concrete embodiment of the agile idea of “small steps, fast runs.”

The SBI, then, is the list of all backlog items the team needs to complete within a Sprint. The SBI is therefore actually extracted from the PBI, distributed as the work the team needs to complete across different Sprints.

Usually, at the Sprint Planning meeting before a Sprint officially starts, the team jointly completes the extraction of the SBI based on the priorities of the PBI and the team’s capacity.

Once the SBI is settled at the planning meeting, it is generally kept as stable as possible. But unexpected situations always arise in reality, and agile embraces change, so a fixed SBI does not necessarily remain constant throughout the Sprint. Based on priority adjustments, and after reaching agreement with the team, the PO can add, remove, or modify items in the SBI—but the prerequisite is that the team reaches consensus.

SBI adjustments usually mean wasted effort, so within a Sprint it should be kept as stable as possible.

The figure shows the SBI already pulled into a Sprint within Jira, a commonly used agile management tool. Once the Sprint begins, the iteration board in Scrum reflects the Sprint’s progress in real time.

Sprint Goal

Similarly, paired with the SBI there is also a supporting artifact, or commitment—the Sprint Goal. This artifact is usually defined by the PO and outlines, at a high level, the core objective the entire Sprint should achieve. After being confirmed and agreed with the team, the Sprint Goal also represents the output the team as a whole commits to delivering in this cycle.

For the various stakeholders not involved in the iteration, the Sprint Goal is also a way to understand the overall progress of the current product.

Increment

Increment means increment. In agile, because of the emphasis on small steps and fast runs, the work output of each iteration is in fact oriented toward the product vision and is an enhancement on top of the existing foundation. It is not only a process of accumulation but also a process of continuously delivering value to users.

Based on agile principles, the Increment should be working software that can demonstrate the product’s value. In other words, the Increment, combined with the outputs of previous Sprints, should always be a forward-looking, minimal usable piece of software—an MVP (Minimum Viable Product)

Whether a Sprint has achieved its Sprint Goal is usually demonstrated at the Sprint Review by showing the functional results of the Increment to relevant stakeholders and obtaining their feedback.

Definition of Done (DoD)

The commitment associated with the Increment is actually the completion status of each backlog item in the SBI. So how is this “done” defined? In Scrum, that corresponds to the DoD. The DoD is a set of common definitions for the main types of backlog items.

In fact, besides the DoD there is also the DoR. The DoR defines under what conditions a backlog item can be considered ready. Only ready backlog items should be pulled into the SBI.

Other Artifacts

In addition to the three core artifacts defined in Scrum and the supporting commitment artifacts, there are also artifacts defined to reflect the status of iteration progress.

Burndown Chart

The Burndown Chart is a visual chart that reflects the progress of a Sprint in a timely manner.

X-axis: the elapsed time of the iteration Y-axis: the workload of the iteration, usually represented by the Story Points estimated in the SBI, reflecting the estimated total effort required to complete the iteration.

Based on the relationship between workload and time, first draw an ideal burndown line of Story Points that is linear, and then draw an actual burndown line based on the work actually completed each day during the iteration. How well these two lines match reflects whether the iteration is currently on track. It is a key iteration status chart that the Scrum Master and the team should keep an eye on at the daily standup.

For this reason, the Burndown Chart is usually regarded as an important artifact in Scrum.

Besides the Burndown Chart, there are in fact many other charts that can be used to analyze current iteration progress. Commonly used ones include:

Cumulative Flow Diagram

The Cumulative Flow Diagram shows the trend of overall requirements moving between different states within a Sprint, and it often plays an important role in identifying team bottlenecks and balancing the workload among members.

Velocity Chart

Another commonly used chart is Velocity. This chart tracks the work completed across multiple Sprints to observe whether the team’s productivity is stable, and thereby forms a basic judgment about the team’s maturity.

The more stable an agile team is, the more constant its output per iteration should be. If the variation fluctuates widely, it indicates that the team still has many problems in task balancing, estimation, and handling interruptions. It is an observational metric.

The above is an introduction to the artifacts—the team’s work objects and deliverables—in Scrum agile. Feel free to keep following this series; updates will continue….

item.title: The Three Core Roles in Scrum
item.description:
In the previous articles of this series, we sorted out the origins of Agile and the main frameworks through which it is put into practice today. Among them, the Scrum framework is the absolute mainstream of Agile practice and is virtually the de facto standard for team-level Agile practice. Most scaled Agile frameworks are also built as extensions on top of Scrum. Therefore, our subsequent summaries will take Scrum as the foundation to explore the main practices and ways of working through which Agile is applied in the software development process.

In this article, we will begin by discussing the composition of roles in the Scrum framework.

The Scrum Team

In Scrum, the Scrum Team exists for one purpose only: every time, it exists to accomplish one valuable goal of the product. As the smallest cohesive unit of productivity in an Agile organization, the Scrum Team has no hierarchy within it. The team is made up of cross-functional professionals, and its members should possess all the skills needed to accomplish the product goal.

In operation, the Scrum Team is responsible for all activities related to the product goal, including collaboration with stakeholders, verification, maintenance, operation, experimentation, research and development, and any other activities that may be needed. The Scrum Team is self-organizing and self-driven, staying focused and continuously delivering value at a sustainable pace.

Although there is no explicit constraint on team size, the ideal size of a Scrum Team should generally be kept to within 10 people. Smaller teams communicate more efficiently and achieve higher productivity per person.

In each iteration (Sprint), delivering a valuable Increment is the responsibility of the entire team. Toward this goal, Scrum defines three different roles within the team: the Developers, the Product Owner, and the Scrum Master.

Product Owner

As the name of the PO role suggests, this person is the owner of the team’s work output — the product. The PO has the final say over what the product should ultimately become. Within the team, the PO is the voice of the end user, and the source, definer, and ultimate decision-maker of requirements.

So the responsibilities of the PO include the following aspects:

1. Defining Requirements and Managing the Product Backlog

The PO’s primary responsibility is, in other words, defining requirements. Requirements are the source of the team’s work and its foundation. Although defining and confirming requirements is not work the PO completes entirely alone — team members also take part in discussing, refining, and improving requirements — the PO is the one who makes the final decision on requirements. The requirements that have been defined constitute the product backlog items, PBI(Product Backlog Item); the PO is the manager and owner of the PBI. Even though the team also participates in maintaining requirement items and refining some technical details, the PO is accountable for every item in the PBI.

The requirements contained in the PBI are a list of all unimplemented requirements, including both near-term and long-term ones. Therefore, when managing the PBI, one of its important attributes is its priority, and defining the priority of PBIs is the PO’s responsibility. Based on the value a requirement brings to the product and on the team’s feedback, the PO weighs risks and benefits to determine the priority order of every requirement.

This is also an inherent advantage of the PBI existing as a list: every requirement has a unique position in the list, and that position represents its priority. The higher up in the list, the higher the priority. An important part of the PO managing the backlog is managing the ordering that corresponds to each requirement. A well-managed PBI is the foundation for starting subsequent iterations.

2. Clarifying Requirements for the Team and Giving Timely Feedback

For an Agile team, since requirements are the input to its work, another important responsibility of the PO is to explain the definition of requirements to the team and to clarify any misunderstandings or descriptions that are not clear or explicit enough.

This process runs continuously throughout development activities. It includes the requirement refinement meeting (grooming meeting) before the Sprint Planning meeting in the early stage, and also the ability to give timely feedback and explanations during the iteration when members have questions about requirements or need a decision. This is also why it is said that a Scrum Team should work together and maintain communication efficiency as an important factor.

3. Maintaining Relationships with Stakeholders

In the course of its work, a Scrum Team inevitably involves a variety of stakeholders, including investors (heads of the various product-related departments), customers, end users, and internal related departments (sales, after-sales, customer service, legal compliance, security, audit, quality, and so on), all of which have some connection to the product. The opinions, voices, and feedback from these different channels may all influence the definition of product-related requirements and their implementation, so the PO is the person responsible for maintaining these channels and communicating and coordinating with these different stakeholders. This is also why the member serving as the PO should be someone with strong communication and collaboration skills.

4. The Confirming Owner of the Work Output (Increment)

As the Owner of the product, whether the team’s work output in each iteration meets the requirements and can achieve the expected product goals is confirmed by the PO.

Although Scrum does not define a separate testing role, the work of testing is in fact included within the Development Team. For the acceptance and confirmation of the product, although the PO makes the final call, that does not mean the PO is responsible for the testing work here. Rather, it is more about judging whether the product goal has been achieved based on the assessment of the testing members or the feedback at the iteration’s demo and review meeting.

All in all, the PO, as a very central role in the Scrum Team, is extremely critical. Having a dedicated person devoted to the role is in fact very necessary. In some Agile projects, the PO may wear several hats and remain detached from the team, which really shows a failure to understand the importance of this role.

Scrum Master

In some dubious Agile projects, people confuse the SM with the traditional project manager (PM), believing that the Scrum Master’s job is the role of a traditional PM. This is a completely wrong understanding.

1. Not the Superior of the Team Members

In traditional projects, the PM is the person in charge of a project and is accountable for its success. At the same time, the PM also holds corresponding project management authority — the authority to assign work to project members and to evaluate their work results — and stands in a different hierarchical relationship from the project members.

But in Scrum, the SM and the team members are peers, with no authority to evaluate or assess them. The SM’s main responsibility is to ensure the smooth progress of the team’s work, acting as a coordinator who, through a professional understanding of Agile and practical experience, guides the team to complete the iteration work as efficiently as possible. The positioning is in fact that of a servant. During the execution of a sprint, by observing and monitoring how the iteration is running, the SM promptly removes impediments, boosts everyone’s morale, and, when necessary, gives the team a shot of adrenaline.

2. Promoting Agile Values and Agile Practices

As the Scurm Master and Agile coach, the SM’s responsibility is to carry through Agile values and convey those values to all members, and through personal practical experience to make the team’s operation conform to Agile principles.

As the facilitator of the Scrum Team, the SM needs to be responsible for organizing some of the main activities in the iteration, most importantly the four ceremonies of Scrum. Of course, this also includes other activities that need coordination and organization, such as discussions of urgent matters, important clarifications, reviews, and so on. In these activities, the SM usually needs to act as the facilitator, ensuring the effectiveness of the activity and keeping it from going off track.

3. The Team’s Firewall

A very critical point in the SM’s responsibilities is that the SM needs to act as the team’s firewall. This is also one of the most challenging aspects of being an SM. For an iteration, achieving the iteration goal is the most important matter for the team during the sprint cycle, and all work in the iteration should revolve around this goal.

But in any organization, it is inevitable that things may arise that interfere with the team members’ work. For example, some leaders may temporarily assign extra tasks, or make temporary transfers of personnel. At such times the SM needs to play the role of a firewall, being able to push these tasks back or, through coordination, seek external support to ensure the current iteration goal is not affected. Everything is aimed at accomplishing the established goals of the sprint and maintaining the team’s fighting capacity, rather than letting team members be directly interfered with by all kinds of external matters that affect the completion of the current iteration’s tasks.

Developers

The main body of the Scrum Team is in fact the Developers Team. But the “developers” here should not be understood as programmers in the traditional sense. The definition of a Scrum Team is that the team should possess all the skills needed to accomplish the product goal, so the Developers Team here is actually a general concept. Besides programmers, it also includes testers, visual designers, and possibly architects, DBAs, configuration management, and many other roles that are distinct in traditional projects — but in Scrum they are all collectively called Developers.

1. Possessing All the Skills Needed to Accomplish the Goal

So for the Developers Team, the primary responsibility is to possess all the skills needed to accomplish the product goal, including design, development, testing, deployment, configuration, and so on. But these tasks are viewed as a whole and are not explicitly mapped to specific individual members. That is to say, the skills of the team members may be comprehensive — specialized in one area yet versatile in many — and the team’s overall capability is not built on dependence on any particular member.

Compared with traditional development, members of a Scrum Development Team should be cross-functional, with each member having the skill requirements and corresponding abilities to take on different types of tasks. Simply put, in this Developers Team, each member’s skills have their own emphasis and they take on corresponding task types, but this is not absolute — they may also need to take on work outside their primary skill area, with everything aimed at accomplishing the iteration’s work goals.

2. Estimating the Backlog and Requirements

Another responsibility of the Development Team is to estimate the backlog items in the PBI.

The implementation of the requirements in the PBI is, after all, the responsibility of the Development Team; the implementation approach, the technology, and the maturity of the team’s capabilities all affect the workload of implementing each requirement.

And the workload of implementing requirements directly affects their completion and delivery, so in Agile, estimating requirements is an important matter.

This estimation is one of the main responsibilities of the Development Team. In Scrum, estimation generally takes place during the requirement clarification meeting or the planning meeting. Methods such as estimation by experience or Planning Poker can be used to assess the implementation complexity and workload of each requirement as objectively as possible.

The accuracy of estimation directly affects the achievement of the iteration goal and the health of the iteration’s operation. It is also an indicator of the maturity of a Development Team.

3. Breaking Down Goals and Claiming Tasks

In the PBI, requirements are mainly business-level demands. But their concrete implementation approach and execution usually still need to be broken down into different tasks, such as front-end tasks, design tasks, back-end tasks, testing tasks, and so on. All of these require the Development Team to complete the task breakdown and, through self-organization, the claiming and assignment of tasks. This work is generally completed collectively by the team during the planning meeting.

4. Fulfilling Commitments and Delivering Value

Finally, there is fulfilling the iteration’s commitment and delivering the product Increment, providing product value. Accomplishing, with both quality and quantity, the established goals committed to during iteration planning is the core of the Development Team’s overall work. The rate at which iteration commitments are met is the most direct indicator for observing whether a Scrum Team is mature and whether Scrum Agile has been successfully implemented.

Summary

The above is a sharing of the three roles in the Scrum framework, along with their respective responsibilities and requirements. Distilled into three sentences:

  • The PO makes sure everyone does the right things
  • The Development Team makes sure things get done
  • The SM makes sure the team does things well

item.title: Agile Development Models You Should Know
item.description:
Preface

In the previous article of this series, What Is Agile? An Overview of Agile, we gave a first introduction to what agility is, the background against which Agile emerged, and why it has become so widely adopted today.

But agility itself is, more than anything, a set of values and a guide at the level of ideas. To apply it in a real organization, you still need concrete practice models to put it into action. As Agile has evolved, a great many different practice models have emerged, and organizing our development process around any of these models can be called Agile Development.

Below, we will focus on sorting out the models that are relatively common in Agile development practice, along with their strengths and weaknesses.

Team-Level Agile

When Agile was first proposed, it started largely from the individual developer’s point of view — the collaborative relationships and development philosophy it hoped to establish in the process of building software and working together. This collaboration was usually the development cooperation inside a single team. So the main practice models of early Agile were primarily aimed at the team level.

Scrum

Scrum was actually proposed quite early. In 1995, Jeff Sutherland and Ken Schwaber first introduced the Scrum framework in their paper “Scrum Software Development Process”. Both of them also took part in signing the Agile Manifesto.

As Agile spread, Scrum came into wide use. According to the latest State of Agile report (17th), Scrum remains the most popular team-level Agile framework today, used by more than 60 percent of the teams surveyed. So it is entirely fair to say that Scrum represents the mainstream practice of Agile.

Our subsequent sharing on Agile practice in this series will also be discussed mainly with Scrum as the reference.

The composition of the Scrum model framework:

  • Core process: a fixed development cycle built around the Sprint
  • Three role definitions: PO, Scrum Master, Dev Team
  • Three artifacts: PBI (Product Backlog), SBI (Sprint Backlog), Increment (product increment)
  • Four work ceremonies: planning meeting, daily standup, review meeting, retrospective meeting

The Scrum framework emphasizes delivering product increments on a regular basis within a fixed, short development cycle (the sprint), using four different work ceremonies to track and coordinate day-to-day work, and it stresses team self-organization and close, flexible collaboration.

Kanban

Kanban actually originated even earlier, growing out of Toyota’s production management theory in the 1940s. It emphasizes using a visual approach to improve efficiency while making the workflow easier to adjust and optimize.

The core principle of Kanban is to clearly display project progress and work allocation to all members through a visual board, to limit the amount of work in progress so as to avoid the waste of resources caused by overload and backlog, and to define and distinguish clear workflows on the board, such as the creation, assignment, execution, testing, and completion of tasks. It emphasizes continuous integration and continuous improvement through regular retrospectives.

Extreme Programming (XP)

Extreame Programming, abbreviated as XP, was proposed by Kent Beck in 1996 and put into practice in the C3 project in which he participated.

The C3 project where Kent Beck practiced XP was a payroll management system for Chrysler. Its participants included several figures who later became important in the Agile movement — for example, two other signatories of the Agile Manifesto, Ron Jeffries and Ward Cunningham, also took part in the project. But the project was in fact not successful: it was delivered several months late, and after running for a while it was shut down completely because of serious performance problems. That is rather ironic.

XP defines 13 practice principles mainly across three dimensions — team operation, the development process, and development technical practices — including continuous integration, pair programming, test-driven development, customer acceptance testing, and so on. It had an important influence on the later Agile Manifesto and the 12 principles of Agile.

Lean Development (Lean)

Lean Development, also known as lean development, likewise grew out of Toyota’s lean production management theory.

It later developed into the software field and mainly includes the following seven core principles:

  • Eliminate Waste

  • Build Quality In

  • Create Knowledage

  • Defer Commitment

  • Deliver Fast

  • Respect People

  • Optimize Whole

Lean puts more emphasis on eliminating waste as much as possible while delivering value to users, and on viewing development from the perspective of the broader business environment.

Crystal Methods (Crystal)

The Crystal method was developed by Alistair Cockburn in 1991 for IBM as a set of guidelines for team collaboration and communication. Alistair Cockburn is regarded as an early popularizer of Agile; after the Agile Manifesto was published, methods including Crystal began to come into public view.

The Crystal methods can be refined into Crystal Clear, Crystal Yellow, Crystal Orange, and Crystal Red. These Crystal methodologies are divided according to the importance of the project and the size of the participating staff.

  • Crystal Clear: teams of around 6 people
  • Crystal Yellow: around 20 people
  • Crystal Orange: around 40 people
  • Crystal Red: around 80 people

The Crystal approach likewise emphasizes seven main characteristics:

1. Frequent Delivery

2. Reflective Improvement

3. Osmotic Communication

4. Personal Safety

5. Focus

6. Easy Access to Expert Users

7. A Technical Environment with Automated Tests, Configuration Management, and Frequent Integration

Compared with XP, Scrum, and the like, Crystal is less disciplined, and its main principles change dynamically depending on team size, so in practice it is not widely applied.

Beyond the five common team Agile frameworks above, there are other team-level Agile practice models such as DSM and FDD, but by far the most widely used today is still Scrum.

Although Agile models are many and varied, in actual application they are not mutually exclusive, because they are, more than anything, ways of putting Agile thinking into practice. Understanding the starting points behind the definitions of these models and learning from each other’s strengths is arguably the more pragmatic way to carry out Agile practice.

Of course, the scale of modern software is growing ever larger, and relying on a single small team alone cannot accomplish system-level development of a software product. These team-level Agile frameworks are usually not suited to organization-level agility when applied to large software systems. For agility at this level, large-scale Agile frameworks have emerged, and in the next article we will continue to share an introduction to this part of the Agile framework landscape.

Large-Scale Agile

The Agile models above grew out of some of the ideas from when Agile was first proposed, and are mainly Agile practices aimed at small teams. But the scale of modern software is growing ever larger, and relying on a single small team alone cannot accomplish system-level development of a software product. So in order to integrate multiple such small teams, the Agile community has proposed a number of different large-scale Agile models.

Compared with Scrum’s absolutely dominant mainstream position in team-level Agile, large-scale Agile frameworks present a scene of a hundred flowers blooming, with no single model occupying an absolute mainstream. Below we introduce several of the better-known scaled Agile frameworks.

SAFe

Based on the latest State of Agile report, SAFe is currently the most widely used large-scale Agile framework, but even it holds only around 22 percent of adoption.

SAFe is short for Sacled Agile Framework; it was born in 2011 and has by now been updated to version 6.0.

It provides a complete structured way to scale Agile practices and offers four different configurations to suit different levels, namely:

  • Essentail: team level (small to medium projects)
  • Large Solution: large solution level (large projects)
  • Portfolio: portfolio level (product lines)
  • Full: organization level (enterprise level)

Within the SAFe framework, on the basis of the Scrum iteration (Sprint), it introduces the concepts of the PI (Program Increment) and the Agile Release Train (ART). A cycle containing several Sprints forms a PI, through which the cooperation of multiple different Scrum teams works together to complete a fairly large-scale product increment.

Beyond the three roles defined by Scrum — PO, Scrum Master, and Dev Team — SAFe defines new roles such as the Product Manager (PM), Release Train Engineer (RTE), Solution Architect (SA), and Business Owner (BO), in order to manage multiple teams, larger-scale product roadmaps, technical architecture, and cross-departmental coordination.

The four core values emphasized by SAFe:

  • Alignment: ensuring everyone in the organization works toward the same direction; clear goals and vision are key.
  • Built-in Quality: focusing on quality from the very beginning to avoid late-stage fixes, ensuring the product meets high quality standards at every development stage.
  • Transparency: creating an open, transparent working environment that encourages communication and feedback among team members.
  • Program Execution: ensuring the smooth delivery of programs and products through a consistent rhythm of development and delivery.

With its fairly complete practice methodology adapted to organizations of different sizes, as well as its broad certification and promotion, SAFe is being applied more and more in the field of scaled Agile today.

SoS

SoS (Scrum of Scrums) is actually a very early scaled Agile model. It was proposed in 2001 — the very year the Agile Manifesto was published — by Scrum co-creator Jeff Sutherland, and was applied in a project practice at GE.

This framework is actually fairly simple to understand.

In essence it is a synchronization mechanism: each Scrum team sends one member, usually called an ambassador, and these people then form a Scurm, that is, the SoS. This team likewise operates according to Scrum principles, with Sprints, standups, a backlog, and so on. But the main concerns of the SoS are cross-team progress, impediments, and coordination.

SoS is also a fairly widely adopted approach in scaling Agile today, but its scale is generally not too large — on the order of 5 to 7 Scrum groups. Above it, SoSoS has been extended, but this further increases the complexity and tends to become chaotic in operation.

NEXUS

Another scaling framework, Nexus, was created by the other proposer of Scrum, the father of Scrum Ken Schewaber, and then launched in 2015 through scrum.org , so it can be regarded as a semi-official scaled Agile framework of Scrum. It was proposed relatively late and is currently little used; the State of Agile report shows an adoption rate of only about 1 percent, so its promotion has not gone well.

Nexus mainly makes a small number of improvements on top of Scrum aimed at cooperation across a larger scope. The framework itself does not change much, and there are likewise just a few differences:

  1. Its main work is done at the cross-team level, including sprint planning, review, and retrospective, but the daily standup is held separately by each subgroup.

  2. A Nexus team is composed of 3–9 Scrum teams; a larger scale becomes hard to organize. These different Scrum groups operate within the same iteration cycle.

  3. Nexus introduces a Nexus Integration Team. This integration team has a function similar to the SoS, mainly responsible for work coordination and progress synchronization among the different Scrum teams.

  4. Nexus shares a single product backlog and has only one PO role; before the planning meeting, a cross-team requirement refinement meeting is held. And the work result is also a single increment.

This framework places very high demands on collaboration between teams, and many matters are jointly completed and synchronized by multiple Scrum groups, so efficiency is hard to guarantee. This is probably the main reason the framework has struggled to gain wider adoption.

LeSS

LeSS (Large-Scale Scrum) is a lightweight Agile framework designed to extend Scrum to multiple teams while preserving Scrum’s core principles and simplicity. It was proposed in 2005 and is also a relatively early framework.

Similar to NeXus, the LeSS Agile framework uses a single product backlog, with all Agile teams working within the same Sprint and collaborating to complete that Sprint.

But in LeSS, there are two Sprint Planning meetings at the start of a Sprint: in the first Sprint Planning meeting, representatives from each team take part in discussing and managing dependencies and collaboration between them. The second Sprint Planning is the Scrum teams’ own Sprint planning. At the end of the Sprint, there are likewise two retrospectives: one is the retrospective within the Agile team, and the other is the retrospective for the entire large-scale Agile project.

LeSS is fairly flexible. Compared with Scrum, it retains all of Scrum’s roles and introduces no new roles, relying more heavily on the team’s ability to self-organize.

Compared with frameworks such as SAFe, LeSS does not introduce extra roles or too many other processes, but scales Agile by simplifying the structure; this, however, also creates difficulties in practical operability when it is implemented. In the latest State of Agile report, its adoption rate stands at 2 percent.

The above is the sorting-out and summary of the various Agile practice models, intended to help everyone gain an overall understanding of the application of Agile and its current state of development.

Thanks for continuing to follow this series — working hard to keep it updated~

item.title: An Overview of Agile: What Is Agile?
item.description:
Agile development is probably the most popular and widely applied development model in today’s IT industry. Yet in actual practice, it always seems to deviate quite a bit from expectations. So I am starting a series to sort out, in detail, the knowledge related to Agile development and to share my own understanding of Agile.

The Origins of Agile

To talk about Agile, we first need to look at the background against which it was proposed.

The Software Crisis

As we know, from the 1970s to the 1990s, computers gradually began to become ordinary consumer goods and started entering households. Taking this as an opportunity, the computer software industry also began to boom and develop rapidly. But at the same time, as the scale of software applications grew, their complexity increased sharply, and a large number of problems caused by software occurred during this period—what is now known as the “software crisis” era.

The software crisis mainly manifested as:

  • Over budget
  • Over schedule
  • Low efficiency
  • Low quality
  • Not meeting requirements
  • Unmanageable, hard-to-maintain code
  • Never able to deliver

To address the problems arising from the software crisis above, software engineering began to develop rapidly as a discipline, and various theories and papers on software development began to emerge. Among them, the Waterfall Model, converted from engineering management in manufacturing, along with its derived V Model and W Model, occupied the mainstream, and their influence continues to this day

The Waterfall Model

But the Waterfall Model also has obvious shortcomings, namely that it is a linear development process, and problems that affect a release often only surface in the later stages. Moreover, this model places very high demands on risk control and values plans and processes, so documentation and standards requirements are extremely strict, and all the red tape also creates big efficiency problems. Cases of software projects failing even while using the Waterfall Model have also remained numerous.

The Rise of the Internet

Another part of the background is the rise of the Internet in the 1990s. Unlike traditional desktop applications, Internet-based applications are delivered the moment they are released, and their user base is enormous. In addition, the free strategy of the Internet makes the cost for users to switch to similar products extremely low, so Internet applications are inherently an industry with extremely frequent requirement changes and very high demands on product iteration and updates. The traditional, process-heavy Waterfall Model had already become very poorly suited to this high-speed demand of Internet products.

It was against exactly the above background that the Agile model emerged.

The History of Agile

Image source: smartSheet

  • As early as the 1940s, Toyota had already adopted quite a few ideas now esteemed in Agile development in its automobile production management. The most typical is Kanban. The main function of this Kanban is to manage the production process and materials through visualization, letting production be driven by demand rather than by early plans.

  • By the 1990s, the Internet began to rise. In 1991, the Crystal methods were proposed; in 1994, Dynamic Systems Development Method (dynamic system develop methodology) DSDM was proposed.

  • In 1995, Scrum was formally proposed as a development model, jointly published by the father of Scrum, Ken Schwaber, and Jeff Sutherland. This is also the most widely applied model in Agile development today, almost synonymous with Agile.

  • In 1996, XP (Extreme Programming) was published, by Kent Beck. He is also the top-ranked luminary among the later signatories of the Agile Manifesto. Many principles in Agile in fact originate from Extreme Programming. As an aside, Kent is also the author of the famous test automation framework Junit. It is fair to say that many later automation frameworks were significantly influenced by Junit.

  • In 2001, the Agile Manifesto was published, jointly signed and released by 17 experts in software development—including Ken, Jeff, Kent, and Martin Fowler—at the Snowbird ski resort in Utah, USA. From then on, Agile gradually moved into the mainstream.

  • 2005, the large-scale Agile framework LeSS (Large Scale Scrum) was proposed

  • In 2006, the first Agile China Conference was held, led by the well-known consulting firm ThoughtWorks.

  • In 2009, the Agile certification system DA (Disciplined Agile) was established

  • In 2011, the large-scale Agile framework SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework) was proposed.

  • In 2018, BizDevOps was proposed, aiming to open up the path from business to R&D.

Developing to the present day, Agile is still spreading widely around the globe, but at the same time, Agile has also exposed some of its own problems, so Agile 2.0 has already begun to be mentioned and discussed.

The Agile Manifesto

In the development of Agile, the publication of the Agile Manifesto was a milestone event. From then on, Agile began to gradually enter the realm of practice and became widely applied

Agile Manifesto Official Website

Individuals and interactions over processes and tools: Agile places more emphasis on the role of the individual, holding that an individual’s subjective initiative is more efficient and useful than relying on processes and tools

Working software over comprehensive documentation: The comprehensive documentation here refers to heavy, rigid documents—red tape that few people actually read once written. Working software, by contrast, means software that can actually run, “seeing once is better than hearing a hundred times”

Customer collaboration over contract negotiation: It emphasizes communication. Developers are the producers of software and customers are the users; more direct communication between the two can better confirm whether what is being built is the same as what you want, rather than agreeing in advance through a so-called contract

Responding to change over following a plan means that change certainly exists, and a good software development process should adapt to that change rather than following a set course to the very end.

The 17 signatories of the Agile Manifesto were all experts with high achievement and prestige in their fields, which also laid a solid foundation for the wide spread of Agile. But these 17 people were mainly experts in the software development field; for the entire software product lifecycle, the absence of other roles also planted limitations in the adaptability of Agile itself.

The 12 Principles of Agile

Besides the Agile Manifesto, Agile also put forward 12 basic principles for practical application

  • Customer satisfaction : Oriented by user value. Customer satisfaction means the value of the software is realized, and software realizing value is the ultimate goal of our developing software.

  • Embrace change: Change certainly exists; rather than controlling change, it is better to accept change.

  • Frequent delivery: Small steps, fast running, rapid delivery, fast feedback, making it easy to correct course in time

  • Mutual cooperation (business and R&D): The business requirement side, user representatives, producers, and the development team should work together. Confirm in time

  • Motivated teams: Self-motivated teams; the team itself is proactive, with no internal friction

  • Face-to-face: Timely communication, seeing once is better than hearing a hundred times

  • Working software: What you see is what you get

  • Sustainable pace: A fixed rhythm better forms tacit understanding

  • Good design (technical excellence): Emphasizing the internal foundation of software development, solving problems through better design, and reducing risk. Emphasizing technical excellence

  • Simplicity is beauty: Software should not be over-engineered; gradually satisfy user needs

  • Self-organizing: Control of the development process should be in the developers’ own hands, without various administrative orders. The father of Scrum, Ken, once clearly stated that the purpose of Agile is to eliminate the manager position.😂😂

  • Reflection and adjustment: This one is a supplement to self-organization. In the course of Agile operation, various failures or rough spots will inevitably occur; at such times it is necessary to review and reflect in time and make timely adjustments and remedies.

The Author’s Views on Agile

Although Agile is widely applied in the industry today, it is not a silver bullet; we still need to view Agile dialectically, for there is no theory or method under heaven that applies everywhere.

  1. The ideas it proposed and some of the principles and practices it developed start from an excellent point, but not all situations are applicable; applying Agile still requires determining the approach based on the actual circumstances of the product and project.

  2. From the Agile Manifesto and principles, it can in fact also be seen that what Agile itself conveys is more a set of values—an ideal direction for software development—rather than a methodology. It is not an execution-level method that guides how a project should operate.

  3. The proposal of Agile was thought through more from the software development angle; it is the conclusions these development gurus reached from a software development perspective. But when Agile is applied in the product domain, many practices are overly idealistic, such as working with customers and self-organizing teams, and especially in traditional enterprises they will face great resistance. It is impossible to advance without a fundamental transformation at the organizational level.

So Agile itself is not a silver bullet, nor is it a methodology. Rather, it is a cultural-level way of thinking; to be applied truly ideally requires organizational-level change to advance, and it is not a practice that can be successfully applied simply by being pushed bottom-up from a small team of a dozen or so people.

On the practical application of Agile, more sharing on the Scurm framework will follow. Stay tuned.

item.title: A Review of Software Branching Strategies and Integration Patterns
item.description:
Preface

Software code is the core asset of any software development team. Branch management is the primary way a team coordinates code synchronization, integration, and conflict resolution among multiple people when collaborating.

This article is compiled from reading notes on the branching model by software guru Martin Fowler.

Base Patterns

Source Branch

All changes are recorded on the same branch.

Definition of a branch: Creating a branch:

Two different developers pull their own development branches based on the main branch:

Jonny LeRoy pointed out that when we draw branch lines, we actually overlook the increase in complexity that builds up over time.

Definition of the Mainline:

Master, Trunk

It is the single shared branch that reflects the current actual state of the product.

You can obtain the current product version state at any time and develop based on it.

Healthy Branch:

Perform automated builds and tests for every commit to ensure no faults are introduced into the current branch (a working, fault-free branch).

Advantages:

  1. A healthy shared branch prevents new branches pulled from it from working on a faulty foundation.
  2. A healthy branch is easier to release directly to production.
  3. Keeping a healthy branch at all times greatly reduces the workload of integration and lowers potential risks.
  4. It facilitates differential debugging. (You can remove the commit that failed debugging and keep only the healthy commits.)
  5. If a problem occurs when integrating into the mainline, you can confirm with certainty that it is caused by a conflict rather than a code error.

It can be a shared branch or your own branch. Self-testing code is the core of a healthy branch; self-tests should produce results quickly (on the order of minutes).

Integration Patterns

Mainline Integration

Developers pull code from the mainline to develop, integrate, and push healthy changes back to the mainline. Pull a branch from the mainline to your local machine and develop on the local branch.

During development, other developers have already committed changes to the mainline branch. At this point, if you want to commit to the mainline, you first need to merge in the other changes. Sometimes there are conflicts between local modifications and already-committed changes; in that case you need to resolve the conflicts first. Then commit the modified, self-tested healthy code back to the mainline branch.

Using a mainline means we will practice the mainline integration pattern.

Feature Branch

Pull an independent branch for each functional feature, and integrate it back into the mainline after the feature is complete.

Pull different feature branches from the mainline and develop on each separately. During development, continuously pull the latest code from the mainline; if there are other feature changes, integrate and resolve conflicts in a timely manner (locally).

After the feature is fully developed, integrate it back into the mainline. (The affected conflicts have already been resolved locally, so all other feature branches can pull the changes directly without any conflicts to resolve.)

Low-Frequency Integration

Several local commits have been made on each of two independent development branches, but they have not been pushed to the mainline. Changes have been merged into the mainline.

The development branches need to pull the changes and merge them into their local branches (resolving conflicts).

On branch A, commits 4 and 5 are completed and then pushed to the mainline. After commits 4, 5, and 6 are completed on branch B, it needs to locally merge in A’s commits from the mainline and, after integration, push to the mainline. (The size of the local merge represents the workload.)

High-Frequency Integration

What if every commit is integrated and pushed to the mainline? V pushes back to the mainline right after completing the first commit.

S performs a local merge right after completing the first commit, and pushes back to the mainline. For S’s second push, there are no changes on the mainline, so there is no local merge work. V completes the second commit and a local merge, then pushes. S’s third commit requires a local merge and a push. In this way, every local commit is pushed to the mainline.

Comparing the two, high-frequency integration involves more local integration work, but the workload of each of these integrations is much lower than that of low-frequency integration. At the same time, more important than the reduced workload is that doing so reduces risk. (Although in most cases a large merge can also be completed smoothly, sometimes there are serious conflict problems that are hard to resolve. In such cases, occasional huge problems are worse than routine small ones.) If each routine integration takes 10 minutes, but 50 integrations combined take 6 hours, it may seem that 6 hours is still less than 500 minutes, but this leads to integration fear (if it hurt, do it more often).

Moreover, under the high-frequency integration model, conflicts between code can be discovered earlier, avoiding the situation where conflicting code is only discovered later, which in the meantime continuously produces a lot of additional conflicting code that should not have existed.

A source control system is actually more of a communication platform, allowing you to be aware of the work of other team members.

Continuous Integration

As soon as a developer completes a healthy commit, they complete mainline integration as quickly as possible, generally within no more than one day.

(If high-frequency integration is more efficient and feasible, but using feature branches means changes are constrained to be no smaller than a feature, then does integration frequency become a problem?)

Continuous Integration - as long as development on a feature is making progress and is healthy, it can be integrated into the mainline. The only rule is that integration must happen every day (or even more frequently).

The development team needs to get used to having unfinished features on the mainline and consider how to avoid exposing these features in the product (by hiding entry points or using configuration control); sometimes we can also implement canary releases.

Under the continuous integration model, developers often do not need to create their own feature branches; they can simply work on the local mainline branch.

The difference between feature branches and continuous integration lies not in whether a feature branch exists, but in when integration into the mainline happens.

A comparison of the two:

The difference between the two patterns depends more on the size of the feature; if a feature is small enough (can be completed within one day), you can practice both feature branches and continuous integration at the same time.

The most obvious problem with feature branches is the workload and uncertainty of merging; however, the bigger problem is that they may prevent refactoring. Refactoring is the most effective way to optimize software, but refactoring creates conflicts, and when the workload of resolving conflicts is too large, refactoring often requires great courage.

Feature Branch Continuous Integration
- All the code in a feature can be evaluated for quality as a single unit
- Feature code is added to the product only after the feature is complete
- Lower merge frequency		 - Supports integration at a frequency higher than the feature length
- Reduces the time to discover conflicts
- Smaller merges
- Encourages refactoring
- Requires commitment to a healthy branch (and thus to self-testing code)
- Scientific evidence shows it helps improve software delivery performance

Feature Branches and Open Source Software

Feature branches on GitHub? The pull request model. Different contexts: distributed, irregular, team members unfamiliar with each other vs. full-time, familiar team members, reliable.

Review of commits

  • Code review·
  • Integration is blocked
  • The importance of modularity

Release Patterns

The mainline branch is the active branch, where code is continuously developed. If the mainline can be kept healthy, anyone can start their work from a stable foundation. And if it is healthy enough, the product can also be released directly from the mainline branch.

For teams practicing CI/CD, a common practice is to track each released version by tagging. But teams that do not practice CD need other release patterns.

Release Branch

A branch prepared for release that only accepts commits aimed at version stabilization and delivery (generally during the system testing phase).

A release branch is pulled from the mainline branch and no longer accepts the merging of any new features. Development work on the release branch mainly consists of fixing discovered bugs or features that affect delivery. All changes eventually still need to be merged back into the mainline. Although the work on a release branch is often smaller in workload than developing new features, if development on it takes too long it can still make merging back into the mainline very difficult (the more commits on the mainline, the harder the merge).

In practice, because of the existence of the release branch, the operation of merging back into the mainline is often easily overlooked, especially when there are difficult conflicts to resolve and release pressure exists.

So some developers adopt another approach: continue developing on the mainline, and then use cherry-pick to merge only release-related commits into the release branch. The drawback of this approach is that cherry-pick is often also difficult in many cases (when there are dependencies on previous commits), and there is often some rework on the release branch before the actual release.

For a team with only one product version, using a single release branch is sufficient. But in many cases there is a need to support multiple product versions; for example, software deployed on a customer’s premises may run on a historical version for a long time, yet still needs ongoing bug fixes or some special requirements. In this case, multiple different release branches need to be maintained and kept in sync with the mainline periodically.

For the development team this clearly greatly increases the maintenance difficulty and workload, but this is more a cost brought about by product strategy. The only thing that can be done is to encourage customers to upgrade to the latest version in a more timely manner (keeping the product stable is critical; once product instability causes problems, it makes customers more inclined to stop upgrading).

Release branches are very necessary for teams that find it difficult to keep the mainline branch continuously healthy; the team can focus on feature validation for product release. But for teams with a single product, release branches are unnecessary; just use the mainline branch and keep it healthy (tag the released versions). In addition, for teams whose release process has many blockers, release branches are also necessary (for example, slow review processes, the launch time windows of app stores, and reviews for security, legal, compliance, etc.).

Maturity Branch

The head of the branch is always marked as the mature code baseline of the most recent version.

Corresponding maturity branches are pulled out according to the team’s different definitions of product maturity. For example, a QA branch (submitted for testing), a Staging branch (pre-release), and a production branch (live).

But in many cases, a clearly defined tagging mechanism can replace the role of maturity branches. For example, “maturity level - internal build number”, “qa-233”, “prod-445”.

Long-Lived Release Branch

A release branch can generally be deleted after the product is released, but we can also maintain a long-lived release branch. Its role can be seen as a combination of a release branch and a maturity branch. Pre-release fixes are done on this branch and merged back into the mainline, and a release tag is added at the actual release, after which preparation for the next version’s release begins.

Environment Branch

Configure the code’s runtime environment through different commits.

Different product runtime environments often have different configuration code (test environment, development environment, performance verification, security verification environment, pre-release environment, production environment, etc.). Environment branches contain the change commits for these configurations and trigger the corresponding builds and deployments.

Environment branches are generally also used as maturity branches; for example, a QA maturity branch will contain the configuration changes for the QA environment.

However, environment branches are not good practice; having different compiled code for different environments introduces risk. If the product program behaves differently in different environments, it makes fixing and locating problems extremely difficult. So it is best to ensure that the executable code running in different environments is identical, and that environment configurations are all controlled through explicit configuration files or variables. Any changes caused by environment changes should not be included in the source control system.

Environment branches should only exist as an emergency mechanism for teams that lack such an environment-switching control mechanism.

Hotfix

A branch used for urgent product failure fixes.

Pull a hotfix branch from the release version corresponding to the mainline branch, and merge it back into the mainline after completion (if the release was a long time ago, the merge work may be considerable). For teams using release branches, a hotfix can also be done directly on the release branch, which is equivalent to turning the original release branch into a hotfix branch. For teams practicing CD, a hotfix can even be completed directly on the mainline (a hotfix branch is still pulled, but from the latest commit), because such teams generally already have the ability to keep unreleased features hidden. Moreover, during the hotfix process, no new commits to the mainline are allowed. (Hotfix takes priority.)

How to define a hotfix? For teams that can release frequently, issues can generally be folded into the regular release cadence without needing a hotfix. It depends on the team’s release frequency and the actual impact on the business.

Release Train

Like a train departing on schedule, there are regular release intervals; after a feature is complete, you choose which release to put it into (this is not the same concept as SAFe’s Agile Release Train, which is more of an organizational-level practice). The team defines a regular release plan and determines the features on each release train, making commitments and arranging their respective work tasks accordingly. Once the train departs, the current branch turns into a release branch and will only accept bug fixes. Release trains are generally used together with feature branches. For teams with many blockers in the release process, the release train is very useful, because these blockers will not affect the development of subsequent features. But the fairly obvious drawback is that if a feature is completed very early, it still has to wait until the departure time to go live.

The release train can be seen as a way to improve a team’s release process. For teams that find it hard to release stably, implementing CD is often not realistic; in that case, the release train is a good choice.

Loading Future Trains

Instead of loading requirements onto a new train only after the old train has departed, a variant of this pattern can be used. If it is uncertain whether some features can be completed before the scheduled departure, two trains can be opened at the same time (with different expected departure times); development work completed on the March train is also committed to the April train, and after the March train departs, the remaining work continues on the April train.

This pattern allows work on the April train to not affect the March train, but the drawback is that if changes on the April train affect the March features, it will make the subsequent merge work more complex.

Comparison with Mainline Release

The main benefit of the release train is having a regular product release calendar, but multiple branches still introduce complexity. In fact, the mainline pattern can work this way too: develop on the mainline, and once the release date arrives, simply add a corresponding release branch.

Release-Ready Mainline

Ensure the mainline is in an absolutely healthy state, and that the head of the mainline can always be released directly to the production environment. (Every commit is healthy enough to be released directly, but only the commits that are actually released need to be tagged.)

Other Release Patterns

Experimental Branch

Collect work used for experiments on the codebase; these features will not be merged directly into the production environment.

Experimental ideas Different ways of implementing a feature

Future Branch

A branch for changes that are too invasive to other branches.

A rarely used pattern that only pulls from the mainline and never merges back into other branches. Once used, it means there is an independent code enclave within the team. The lifetime of this branch should be kept as short as possible.

Collaboration Branch

Used for collaborative work between developers in situations where no formal integration is needed.

Team Integration Branch

Allow sub-teams to integrate with each other before integrating into the mainline. (Large projects.)

Original reference: Martin’s blog Branch Patterns

item.title: Understanding the Cultural Logic Behind the Agile Manifesto
item.description:
Agile is now a widely adopted development philosophy and mindset. The famous Agile Manifesto has been widely circulated and translated into more than 60 languages.

This manifesto primarily presents certain values in software development that these pioneers considered more important, conveying a new philosophy different from traditional development approaches.

But what is the logic behind these proposed principles?

We should understand why such a manifesto exists; otherwise, while everyone claims to be practicing Agile, there’s some ambiguity, and sometimes people even create many processes, ceremonies, and various Agile tools in the name of Agile, ultimately coming full circle back to where they started.

Here, I attempt to understand the underlying logic and true purpose of the Agile Manifesto. By grasping this core concept, we can understand the essence of Agile.

Culture is the Core of Agile

The values promoted in the Agile Manifesto - individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration, responding to change - are not specific practices but rather values.

And values are essential elements in establishing culture.

Any organization, when it reaches a certain stage, will begin to emphasize the importance of culture.

Because mature organizations, after standardized development and establishing mature systems, find that there are still many things that cannot be well resolved through systems alone. At this point, the hoped-for solution lies in the power of culture.

Agile emerged as a response to traditional development processes that heavily relied on procedures and systems. Based on numerous experiences and lessons where software development couldn’t succeed through processes and standards alone, Agile proposes to guide people in establishing the right software development culture at a cultural level, actively improving rather than denying the role of existing processes and standards.

So, the conclusion of this reflection is:

Agile is actually a mindset shift, a set of values for establishing correct behaviors in software development. While implementation methods may vary greatly, the essence is emphasizing that establishing correct development values is more important than specific processes and standards.

Culture is the Evolution of Systems

Understanding Agile as an effort to establish culture helps us understand the logic behind various Agile practices and advocated approaches.

Culture and systems are the pillars supporting an organization’s development. They both aim to guide organization members to do things correctly:

  • Systems guide members through various written rules and processes. Following systems to do things is passively doing things correctly
  • Culture works through gradual influence, with organization members sharing common missions, visions, and values, reflected in their behavior patterns. It’s actively doing things correctly.

What is Culture?

Culture is actually the behavioral patterns of organization members in practice.

Understanding corporate culture also includes elements like mission, values, vision, and strategy.

Their relationship can be summarized in the following diagram:

Coming back to Agile:

The Agile Manifesto represents values The 12 Agile Principles are implementation strategies The Agile vision, like all products, is to deliver value to users

Ultimately, what Agile hopes to achieve is establishing a new culture oriented towards software development.

Like water has no constant form and warfare has no constant conditions, Agile has no so-called standard practices. A team that aligns with Agile values, reaches consensus, and puts them into practice is an Agile team.
